prize_parts.citation: for the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles, built on lipid polymorphism, pH-controlled charge and controlled self-assembly, that deliver nucleic-acid medicines into cells

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B069 to B045. The reason is the weight of the first-round exchange, not a change in how I rate condensates as a concept. B045 is a case where a physical-chemical principle was turned into a working design rule and then validated at large scale. Lipid polymorphism, pH-dependent charge on an ionizable headgroup, and rapid-mixing self-assembly together solve the problem of getting a large, charged, fragile polyanion into the cytosol. That solution has been replicated by many groups and has produced approved siRNA therapy and billions of mRNA vaccine doses. It is the most mature and best validated of the achievements that sit in lipid and colloid chemistry, which is the area of the shortlist I can judge most directly. The credit can be written narrowly: the Vancouver line (Cullis, with Hope and Madden) holds the liposome-to-ionizable-lipid-to-rapid-mixing sequence that is the mechanism of the delivery, and a citation worded around that mechanism says something the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification does not say, since that prize concerned the cargo and not the vehicle.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the largest weakness. MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer each have a credible claim, and any three-name cut will be criticised, especially because part of the translational chemistry sits in industry. The 2023 Medicine prize makes the public association with mRNA vaccines strong, so the citation must be about the lipid chemistry and delivery of nucleic acids in general, with siRNA as the first clinical proof. I also have to weigh my own field closeness to lipid self-assembly, which could make me favour a lipid-based discovery. Finally, I give up a more conceptual contribution in B069 for a more applied one, and I accept that cost because B069 does not currently have a defensible path to five votes or a clean three-name credit.

responses.point: Linke argues that the interpretation of condensates in vivo is contested, which is a deeper maturity problem than stability for perovskites, and that the credit split among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag is unstable.
responses.response: I partly concede this point. I still think the in vitro thermodynamics of multivalent demixing is chemistry, but I cannot show that a three-name cut is stable when Pappu and Mittag supplied the sequence-level grammar, and a prize that must hedge on what is liquid inside a cell is weaker than one with a settled outcome. That is the main reason I have moved off B069 and kept it only as an alternative. I do not move to B016. My question stays that of round 1: the lead and stability caveats you accept for perovskites are of a different kind from the interpretive dispute for condensates, but they are also real, and Aili, Aqvist, Brzezinski and Chabes treat them as an early-recognition problem. I would like to know whether you consider the photophysics and defect chemistry of the absorber, rather than device efficiency, to be what the citation honours, because that wording would make it much easier for me to see it as chemistry.

responses.point: Aili asks whether the lipidoid and combinatorial strand (Langer, Anderson) is chemically decisive or only supportive, and accepts that Hope or Madden could replace Langer if the committee stays within the ionizable-lipid and rapid-mixing line.
responses.response: Thank you for the direct question. My view is that the lipidoid strand is supportive and not decisive. Combinatorial screening broadened the set of lipids that work, and it deserves a place in the history. But the mechanism that makes any of them work is what the Vancouver group established: charge that is neutral in the circulation and cationic in the endosome, the non-bilayer phase behaviour that drives membrane fusion and release, and the controlled self-assembly that encapsulates the nucleic acid. A citation that credits the mechanism is more defensible than one that credits the breadth of the screening. I therefore propose that we converge on the Vancouver trio, and I would accept Cullis and Hope or Madden as a pair only if the committee wants to keep a name free for another part. I recognise this means moving closer to your first choice but not to your pair, and I am open to hearing evidence that Langer's role was decisive for the first clinical products.

responses.point: Zou accepts that B045 applies lipid polymorphism and pH-dependent charge with stronger clinical validation than perovskites, but doubts the chemistry-specific attribution to Cullis, Hope and Madden because delivery came from liposomes, lipidoids and industrial formulation by many groups and the 2023 Medicine prize overlaps.
responses.response: I accept that the attribution has to be argued and that the field is collective. I would answer in two parts. First, the choice of three names is a statement about which step is the mechanism, not a claim that nobody else contributed, and Madden and Hope's work on ionizable lipids and on rapid mixing is the part that can be traced to a specific physical-chemical insight. Second, on the 2023 prize, that recognition concerned modified nucleosides that evade innate immunity. Without a vehicle, neither siRNA nor mRNA would reach the cytosol, and the citation can say so without repeating that prize. If you still consider the attribution too uncertain, I would ask what you would need to see in the expert reports to treat the Vancouver line as distinct, since your own round-1 ranking placed perovskites on the strength of a clean chain of credit.

responses.point: Aqvist holds that Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics has the cleanest two-person attribution and the longest validation, while conceding that Born-Oppenheimer MD now does much of what the fictitious-dynamics scheme did and that a third computational prize may be too much.
responses.response: Your own case against B029 is the one I find persuasive. If the lasting practice is Born-Oppenheimer MD with efficient density-functional theory, the citation would honour a conceptual step more than a continuing method, and the 1998 and 2013 prizes already cover much of the territory. I keep B029 as an alternative because its attribution is the cleanest on the list, but I do not think it can be our central configuration while the question put to you by the chair, which results truly depend on the fictitious-dynamics formulation, remains unanswered.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the Vancouver trio as the decisive line for ionizable lipid nanoparticles, or insists that Langer, Anderson or MacLachlan be credited.
Whether a citation about lipid chemistry and nucleic-acid delivery is sufficiently separate from the 2023 Medicine prize in the eyes of members who see the two as adjacent.
Whether B069 will reach a settled in vivo picture and a stable credit split in a later year, which I now think is more likely than for this year's ballot.
Whether my closeness to lipid self-assembly leads me to overweight the physical-chemical mechanism and underweight the contribution of combinatorial screening.
statement.conflict_note: My research on lipid self-assembly, membrane phase behaviour and lipid-protein co-assembly is close to B045 and to B069, and I declare a field bias toward soft matter and lipid chemistry. I know none of the credited individuals from my profile and have no collaboration or personal tie to the Vancouver group or to any other credited name. I serve with Lund colleagues Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, which I do not treat as a recusal ground for these candidates. I do not seek recusal, but because the lipid area is my own, colleagues should weigh my judgment on B045 with that in mind.
